content: Sulindac is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that may increase the risk of heart attack or stroke, particularly in individuals who take it for extended periods. These cardiovascular events can occur without warning and may be fatal. Inform your doctor if you or your family have a history of heart disease, heart attack, or stroke, if you smoke, or if you have high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or diabetes. Seek emergency medical attention immediately if you experience chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. Do not take sulindac before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Sulindac and other NSAIDs can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines, which may occur at any time during treatment, often without warning symptoms, and can be life-threatening. The risk is higher for individuals who take NSAIDs long-term, are older, in poor health, or consume large amounts of alcohol. Notify your doctor if you are taking anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., prednisone). Also, inform your doctor if you have a history of stomach or intestinal ulcers, bleeding disorders, or other bleeding issues. Stop taking sulindac and contact your doctor if you experience stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for monitoring. Your doctor will carefully assess your symptoms and may order tests to evaluate your response to sulindac. Communicate openly with your doctor about how you feel to ensure the medication is prescribed at the lowest effective dose to minimize serious side effects. You will receive a Medication Guide from your doctor or pharmacist when starting sulindac and with each prescription refill. Read this information carefully and ask any questions you may have. You can also visit the FDA or the manufacturer’s website for additional details. Sulindac is prescribed to relieve pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness associated with osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. It is also used to treat shoulder pain caused by bursitis or tendinitis and to alleviate gouty arthritis symptoms. Sulindac belongs to the NSAID class of medications and works by inhibiting the production of substances in the body that cause pain, fever, and inflammation. Sulindac is available as an oral tablet and is typically taken with food twice daily. Take it at the same times each day, following your doctor’s instructions precisely. Do not take more or less than prescribed. Sulindac helps manage arthritis pain but does not cure the condition. It may take a week or longer to feel the full benefits of the medication. Sulindac is sometimes used to reduce the number of polyps in the colon and rectum in patients with familial adenomatous polyposis, a condition that increases the risk of colon cancer. Discuss the risks and benefits of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Sulindac may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking sulindac, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to sulindac, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention medications listed in the Important Warning section, as well as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, cyclosporine, diuretics, lithium, oral diabetes medications, methotrexate, and probenecid. Notify your doctor if you have or have ever had asthma, nasal polyps, kidney stones, swelling in the extremities, or liver or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, especially in the last months of pregnancy, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking sulindac, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking sulindac. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking sulindac. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Sulindac may cause mild side effects, including headache, dizziness, nervousness, diarrhea, constipation, gas, or ringing in the ears. Inform your doctor if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects may include unexplained weight gain, fever, chills, cough, sweating, muscle or joint pain, chest pain, blisters, rash, itching, hives, swelling of the face or extremities, difficulty breathing or swallowing, hoarseness, pale skin, rapid heartbeat, unusual bleeding or bruising, fatigue, stomach pain, loss of appetite, flu-like symptoms, yellowing of the skin or eyes, discolored or bloody urine, back pain, painful urination, or vision problems. Stop taking sulindac and contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Report serious side effects to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store sulindac in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include loss of consciousness, fainting, dizziness, blurred vision, upset stomach, or decreased urination. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
